# Independent audit of the centered-line comparison

Audited source: `candidate ceb2615ce03b7dbc`.



Let a nonzero integrable log-concave function f have 0 in the interior of its positive support, with c=f(0)>0, and centroid 0. With S=integral f, I=integral_{x>0} x f(x)=integral_{x<0}(-x)f(x), and L=2 sqrt(2I), the source proves

    sqrt(c/2) <= S/L <= sqrt(c).

If f=h^m on its support with h concave and m>=1, the lower bound improves to

    sqrt[c(m+2)/(2(m+1))] <= S/L.

The upper constant is attained by a centered constant interval; the power lower constant by a symmetric power tent; the log-concave lower constant by a symmetric two-sided exponential.

## 1. Integrability and supporting slopes

An integrable log-concave function positive on a neighborhood of 0 has finite moments of every order. For completeness, on any unbounded positive-support ray there must be a point at which log f has fallen below its value at an earlier point, or integrability fails. The corresponding negative secant slope, together with concavity, bounds every later value by a decaying exponential. The opposite ray is identical after reflection. Thus the centroid and first absolute moment are unambiguous, and I is finite and strictly positive.

Since log f is finite and concave on an open interval about 0, it has a finite supporting slope there. Its supporting affine function is an upper bound on the entire positive support. The proof therefore does not require that 0 be a mode. Values at support endpoints do not affect the integrals.

## 2. Entropy-width monotonicity

For F(t)=t log t-t+1 and G(t)=(t+1)/2-integral_0^1 t^s ds,

    F''(t)=1/t,
    G''(t)/F''(t)=integral_0^1 s(1-s)t^(s-1) ds.

This ratio is strictly decreasing for t>0. Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at 1. On t>1, G/F is the mean of G''/F'' with weight (t-x)F''(x), 1<x<t. When t increases, the relative density on the common interval is increasing in x and all new mass lies to the right. Both changes decrease this mean. On t<1, use (x-t)F''(x), t<x<1: increasing t removes the leftmost interval and gives an increasing relative density on the remainder, again decreasing the mean. Its common limit at 1 is 1/6. This justifies monotonicity on the entire positive line, not only separately on the two sides.

For F(a)=F(b)=u, 0<a<1<b, write A=-log a and B=log b. Direct substitution gives

    w=b-a,
    w'=1/A+1/B,
    u w'=w-(b-1)/B+(1-a)/A.

Thus G(b)<=G(a) is exactly 2u w'<=w. The resulting bound w^2<=8u has the correct direction. The limit at u=0 uses F(1+t)=t^2/2+O(t^3); the endpoint u=1 is a=0, b=e and follows continuously.

## 3. Two bathtub bounds

After normalization f(0)=1 and reflection, take a supporting log slope s>=0. For s=0, the envelope f<=1 separately on both rays yields at most sqrt(2I) mass per ray. For s>0, the decaying-ray envelope forces u=s^2 I<=1. The two filled-envelope candidates have cutoffs A/s and B/s defined by

    u=1-(A+1)e^(-A)=(B-1)e^B+1.

For any competitor h and its filled candidate g, h-g is nonpositive before the cutoff and nonnegative afterwards. Consequently integral x(h-g)>=cutoff integral(h-g); the equal first moments force the desired upper mass bound. At A=infinity the whole-envelope mass bound suffices. Summation yields sS<=b-a<=sqrt(8u). Rescaling f restores sqrt(c), with no missing factor of c.

## 4. Lower bounds by one crossing

For h concave, h(0)=1 and f=h^m, an integrable positive-support ray has a finite endpoint b. The matched tent g=(1-t/a)_+^m has I=a^2/((m+1)(m+2)). If b>a, concavity between 0 and a gives f>=g on [0,a] and strict extra moment, a contradiction. For b<=a, the quotient of h(t)-(1-t/a) by t is nonincreasing on (0,b). Extending f by zero gives a positive-to-negative crossing for f-g. At a crossing t0,

    integral t(f-g)<=t0 integral(f-g),

so equal first moments imply integral f>=integral g. If there is no crossing and the first moments agree, the functions agree almost everywhere; thus no division by a zero crossing is needed.

The same proof for log-concave f uses log f+t/a and the matched exponential g=e^(-t/a), I=a^2. The finite first absolute moments proved above justify integrating the crossing inequality even for unbounded supports. Summing the two rays gives exactly the stated constants.

## 5. Scope of the comparison

The radial chord construction preserves central halfspace fractions and turns a line with zero first moment into a centered chord. The comparison controls only the ratio of line mass to chord length. It does not identify the original full centroid, preserve the section-normal balance, or establish a joint inequality involving the cap fractions and these ratios. The source explicitly retains this limitation.
